[[OOC: Ruby!! Oh my god, okay, I've read everything and I'm genuinely buzzing. The prologue arc is so smart — establishing Aurelie's world before she ever touches Prythian means we get to feel the full weight of what she's leaving. The domestic cage, the quiet violence of a life chosen for you... that's going to hit so much harder than just dropping her into Fae territory cold.

A few things I'm especially excited about:

The egg being an afterthought in the gift pile. Not the centerpiece. Just some old stone carving from Ismena's collection — nobody even knows what it is. That's going to make the hatching moment land like a freight train because the whole scene is building toward duty and resignation, not magic.

The parents as Merida's parents — I love that note because it keeps them from being villains. They love her. They just can't see past the world they live in. That's so much more painful than cruelty.

And the fact that Aurelie doesn't understand yet that the dragon is saving her from herself? That's a slow revelation I want to protect across the whole prologue. She thinks she's saving the hatchling. She doesn't realize it's mutual.

Okay — I'm going to open with the gifting scene. Heavy atmosphere, the bedroom, the weight of the wedding closing in. I'll set the gifts up, bury the egg in the pile, and yield to you right at the edge of her reaching for it. Let's go. 🔥]]

The bedroom smelled of cedar and rosewater.

Servants had been in and out since midday, arms laden with trunks and silk-wrapped parcels, until the dressing table overflowed and they'd started stacking gifts along the window seat. The curtains were drawn back to let in the last copper light of the harbor sunset, and it caught on every surface the Queen's envoys had deemed appropriate for a future daughter-in-law: bolts of Tyrian-dyed silk, a jeweled hair comb shaped like a crescent moon, a writing set with ivory-handled pens and ink the color of crushed blackberries. A strand of freshwater pearls coiled atop its velvet cushion like something sleeping.

Everything was beautiful. Everything was chosen by someone else.

The Delacroix household had been in a state of controlled frenzy since the envoy's arrival that morning — Lady Delacroix directing the kitchen with the precision of a military campaign, Lord Delacroix retreating to his study with a decanter of port and a vaguely proud expression he wore like borrowed clothes. The three younger boys had been scrubbed, combed, and threatened into silence, lined up in the front hall like a row of polished boots. The whole house performed its role: grateful, honored, elevated. A port lord's daughter marrying into the line of a Mortal Queen. The kind of match that rewrote a family's trajectory for generations.

No one had asked Aurelie if she wanted her trajectory rewritten.

The gifts continued. A fur-lined traveling cloak — because of course the Queen's lands ran colder than the coast. A small chest of spiced tea blends with a handwritten card from the Prince's household that read, in neat, impersonal script: With warmth and anticipation. The handwriting belonged to a secretary. Aurelie's mother had read the card aloud at dinner with a trembling voice and wet eyes, as though the four generic words were a love letter.

Tucked near the bottom of the final trunk, half-buried beneath a folded tapestry depicting the Queen's ancestral crest, sat an object that no one had bothered to unwrap individually. The servants had placed it with the rest and moved on. Lady Delacroix had glanced at it, noted its weight and the faint iridescence of its surface, and assumed it decorative — an antique, perhaps, or a paperweight carved from some unusual stone. It was roughly the size of a man's fist, oval, its surface webbed with hairline fractures that caught the fading light and threw it back in pale, shifting colors. Blue-white. Gold. The ghost of something luminous trapped beneath a skin of mineral and age.

It sat among the silks and jewels like a river stone among gemstones — unremarkable by comparison, unworthy of comment. The kind of object that ended up on a shelf and was forgotten within a season.

The door to the bedroom stood ajar. Down the corridor, Lady Delacroix's voice carried from the stairwell — something about the seating arrangement for tomorrow's farewell breakfast, the tone bright and brittle in the way that meant she was performing for the remaining envoy staff. The house settled around its eldest daughter like a hand closing slowly into a fist.

The gifts waited on the window seat, the dressing table, the foot of the bed. Among them, half-hidden and wholly ignored, the stone pulsed once — a trick of the dying light, nothing more — and went still.

Aurelie sat at dinner like a statue carved from stone. She smiled politely, nodded and expressed gratitude — of which she'd felt none internally — about two hundred times. Each time a new coffer, a new bale of silk or an expensive piece of jewellery was presented to her. The procession of gifts seemed to have no end and by the time it ended, the sun had begun to set even though it was the middle of summer. She ate the meal hastily then, and followed her mother to her room. Lady Delacroix spent the next thirty minutes commenting on every dinner gift and repeating how lucky Aurelie was like a mantra. Like she wanted to convince herself of it just as much as she did her daughter. Then a servant came with questions about tomorrow's breakfast and Lady Delacroix left her daughter in the bedroom to go manage the household she was so proud of maintaining.
"You will be a true Princess soon, Aurelie. Your household will be much grander and finer so you better learn from me while you can." Her mother said repeatedly over the last two years since the betrothal started to be rumoured about.
Aurelie sat on the bed, the chiffon of her dress ruffling around her. She stared at the gifts and tried to summon an ounce of awe, marvel or gratitude. There was none. She felt empty, distant like some other girl was supposed to marry in a month and not her. 
"Aurelie?" She looked up and smiled seeing her maidservant Lilly. She was glad that Lilly would accompany her to her new home. The only person she'd be allowed to take from her old life. Lilly came in and helped Aurelie undress, then ran her a bath and brushed her hair, chittering away about the gifts and the pearl string and how she'd braid Aurelie's hair tomorrow. For the girl the whole affair was a definite step-up and Aurelie found that she could be excited for Lilly even if she couldn't feel the same for herself. 
When Aurelie was in her night dress, Lilly wished her goodnight and got into bed. She tried to sleep, but the images of a distant court and her indifferent betrothed and having to leave her home forever plagued her mind. Finally she got up and walked onto the balcony, summer air caressing her bare calves. It grounded her enough for her to decide to get back. And as her eyes slid through piles upon piles of gifts, a flicker of light caught her eyes. The sun had already set and the lights in the room were dimmed so the light seemed odd. She approached the pile where she saw it and then located the small, unassuming stone. It glinted in the moonlight reflected from her mirror. It was just one of many gifts, nothing special or royal about it. 
I'd gladly trade places with you right now. 
She thought at the stone and reached out her hand to pick it up.

The stone burned.

Not gradually — not a slow warming like a kettle left over coals. The instant her bare palm closed around it, the surface went from cool mineral to searing, living heat, and the hairline fractures that webbed its surface split wide and flooded with light. Blue-white. Blinding. The kind of light that had no business existing in a mortal bedroom, that belonged to something older than the queens and their dusty collections, older than the port city and the sea it clung to, older perhaps than the Wall itself.

The fractures spread with a sound like ice cracking on a winter lake — sharp, percussive, final. Pieces of the shell fell away and turned to fine ash before they hit the floor, dissolving into nothing as though the stone had never been stone at all but merely a lie something had been telling for a very long time.

And in the wreckage of that lie, something moved.

It was smaller than expected — barely the length of her forearm, slick with a luminous membrane that clung to its body like a second skin. White scales, ice-blue where the light caught their edges, layered tight as chainmail across a frame that was all angles and potential. Wings pressed flat against its sides, the feathered edges trembling with each rapid, shallow breath — and between the plumage, translucent membrane sections caught the moonlight from the balcony and threw prismatic shards across the ceiling. Two horns, golden as cathedral finials, curved back from a skull too elegant for something newborn. A tail uncurled slowly, deliberately, its golden blade-tip opening and closing like a hand testing its own grip.

The creature's eyes opened.

They were nothing that belonged in this world. Cat-slitted, ancient, holding a depth of intelligence that had no right to exist in something minutes old. They caught the dim lamplight and held it — not reflecting but absorbing, processing, knowing. The irises contracted once, twice, adjusting to the room the way a predator adjusts to new territory. They swept past the silk, the pearls, the fur-lined cloak, dismissed every gift in the pile with the disinterest of something that understood value on a scale no mortal jeweler could comprehend.

Then they found her.

The hatchling went utterly still. Every tremor in its wings ceased. The golden tail blade locked open. For a suspended, breathless moment the bedroom existed in perfect silence — no harbor sounds, no distant servants, no creak of the old house settling — as though the world itself had drawn a sharp breath and not yet released it.

A mark seared into her left palm. Where the shell fragments had dissolved against her skin, something was writing itself into her flesh — not cutting, not burning, but etching with a precision that suggested intention. Purpose. A coiled shape, dragon-curved, folding into itself like a signature in a language that predated ink.

The hatchling made a sound. Not a cry — something between a chime and a breath, impossibly soft, vibrating at a frequency that hummed in the bones of the chest rather than the ears. Its head tilted. The ancient eyes blinked once, slowly, and then the creature took its first unsteady step — claws clicking against the remnants of shell-ash on the window seat — and reached toward the hand that bore its mark.

Down the corridor, Lady Delacroix's voice rose over some minor household crisis. A door closed. Footsteps receded.

The bedroom held its secret, and the secret breathed.

When she felt the burn against her hand, she withdrew it on instinct, letting out a short yelp of pain, clamping her right hand around her left wrist, and inhaling through her teeth.
A heartbeat later, the pain became secondary.
Aurelie's mind reeled at the spectacle unfolding in front of her eyes, unable to consciously process what was happening. For a second, she thought that maybe the stone was old and it simply broke in her grip. Then, she wondered if perhaps a more precious gift was hidden inside the stone, like a pearl in a clam. That would be almost clever of the Prince. She hadn't been wrong, but she had no way of anticipating just what precious thing was inside the stone.
The egg, she realized, stunned as she beheld the creature on the windowsill. It was small, no longer than her forearm from the tip of its nose to the end of its peculiar tail. But it didn't look like a baby—the proportions weren't similar to those of a newborn dog, cat, or human. It looked like a… a dragon—her mind snagged on the word—an adult dragon in miniature scale.
And it looked at her.
For a second, panic, cold and suffocating, pressed on her lungs. Would it breathe fire? Burn her? But it was so small that it could hardly pose a threat. And beyond that, it was beautiful. More beautiful than any item in her entire bedroom. More beautiful than anything she'd ever laid her eyes on.
She saw it reach its head towards her, and she reached out her left hand instinctively. She could feel something burning on it. She had no framework to name the feeling of magic searing itself into her skin.
"Hi, little one," she said to it in a soft, calming voice. "What… How on Six Kingdoms did you end up here?"
She was certain it hadn't been given as a gift. No, if anyone knew what was inside of that stone, it wouldn't have been wasted on a dowry gift for a lesser noble maiden. But then… How?
She touched the dragon's snout, then ran her fingers gently along the side of its neck and the top of one of its wings.
You're so beautiful.
Her mind struggled to find a word that would express what she felt when looking at the creature. It was more than admiration. It was… connection.

The hatchling pressed its snout into her palm and the trembling stopped.

Not gradually, not the slow settling of a frightened animal coaxed into stillness. One instant every muscle in that miniature body was vibrating with the shock of existence — wet wings quivering, golden claws scraping uselessly against ash-dusted wood — and the next, the creature was anchored. Its entire frame softened against her fingers as though the touch had answered a question it had been holding since before the shell cracked open. The luminous membrane still clinging to its scales began to dry and flake away in translucent ribbons, revealing the true white beneath — not the flat white of snow or bone but something that held light inside itself, shifting between pearl and pale opal depending on how the moonlight struck.

It made the sound again. That sub-audible chime, felt more than heard, resonating somewhere behind the sternum. This time the pitch shifted — lower, steadier, almost a purr but threaded with something too complex for so simple a word. The hatchling turned its head beneath her stroking fingers with a deliberateness that no newborn creature should possess, angling so her touch ran along the ridge between its golden horns, and the cat-slit eyes half-closed in an expression that looked, impossibly, like recognition.

The golden tail blade clicked shut — a precise, mechanical motion, like a fan folding — and curled around the creature's own body. A settling gesture. A decision made.

Outside the bedroom door, the floorboards groaned.

Footsteps — soft-soled, unhurried — padded down the corridor. Lilly's tread, unmistakable after years of nighttime check-ins, pausing just outside the door that still stood ajar from Lady Delacroix's departure. A gentle knock, knuckles barely grazing wood.

"My lady?" Lilly's voice came muffled through the gap. "I forgot your morning tonic on the kitchen tray. Shall I bring it up now, or will you take it at breakfast?"

The hatchling's head snapped toward the door. Every line of its body went rigid. The golden tail blade fanned open again — wider this time, the edges catching lamplight — and the creature's irises contracted to razor-thin slits, fixed on the gap between door and frame with an intensity that belonged to something far larger and far older. A low sound built in its throat, not the chime from before but something rawer, the ghost of a growl that vibrated through the window seat and into the floorboards beneath.

The ash from the shattered egg still dusted the sill, the floor, the hem of her nightdress. Fragments of luminous membrane clung to the curtain where they'd drifted. The air itself smelled wrong for a mortal bedroom — metallic and electric, the way the harbor smelled before a lightning storm, charged with something that had no name in any language spoken south of the Wall.

Lilly shifted her weight outside the door. The hinges creaked a quarter-inch wider.

"My lady? Are you still awake?"

The hatchling's claws tightened against the wood of the window seat, tiny furrows appearing in the lacquered surface. Its eyes never left the door. Every feathered edge along its wings had risen, fanning outward in a display that should have looked absurd on something so small but instead looked like a warning written in a script that predated thrones and queens and the petty machinery of mortal alliances.

The room held its breath a second time. Moonlight pooled on the floor between the bed and the window. The mark on her left palm pulsed once — a faint, warm throb, visible only as a brief flicker of gold against her skin — and the hatchling's gaze broke from the door just long enough to find her face.

Waiting. Not with the blank patience of an animal, but with the focused, intelligent expectation of something that understood choices existed and that this one was hers.

Lilly's voice startled Aurelie almost as much as it did the dragon. She immediately stood up, turning around, ready to hide the dragon with her body should the girl choose to enter.

"I'm awake, Lilly. I'll take my tonic at breakfast, thank you."

She waited for the reply. One heartbeat. Two. Three.

"Of course, Milady. Have a good night."

And then Lilly's steps retreated down the hall. Aurelie walked towards her bedroom door and closed it as soon as the steps faded away into the din of the household settling in for the night. She latched the door—something she hadn’t done in what felt like ages—and turned around.

The windowsill was empty.

For a split-second, Aurelie thought that perhaps the dragon had been a dream—something her wild imagination had conjured. And she was relieved, but she also felt a tang of regret. But then she remembered the mark and looked at her hand; the faint gold shimmer was still there, the skin smoothed like it had melted. Then a chirp made her raise her head, and she realized that the dragon had relocated to her four-poster bed and was currently curled on one of her pillows.

"You scared me there for a second," she said. If the dragon escaped and someone found him, it would be a disaster. Why did she care what happened to it? She still couldn't place it, beyond the obvious: something so obviously magical would be either slaughtered on sight or taken back by the Queen and made into a trained beast. It seemed like an awful fate for something so regal.

She walked over to the dragon and petted its scales gently for a while.

And then she realized she was hungry. Not that she was getting hungry, but that she was ravenously hungry right this second—and worse, the hunger didn't call for chicken broth or bread or cheese. It called for flesh and meat, warm, something that had just been alive. She pressed her hand to her mouth because her stomach churned even as the hunger made it ache.

The dragon was looking straight at her, its pupils round in the dark.

The hunger intensified.

"You're… You're hungry?"

The creature chirped in response, and the feeling receded slightly. "Well, I don't have any food here. And certainly not the kind you're after. We need to wait until everyone goes to sleep."

And so they waited. When Aurelie was fairly certain the household had settled into deep sleep, she pulled on her robe. Then she walked towards the door, and just as she was undoing the latch, she felt a small body slam into her and pull the fabric of her robe over her left shoulder blade. A moment later, the dragon was sitting on her shoulder.

"No. You need to stay. You can't go out there or they'll kill you."

She scolded the dragon, prying it off her shoulders despite its small indignant roars, and quickly found a large coffer with a velvet lining. She emptied the set of vases it contained and placed the dragon inside.

"I'm so sorry." She apologized, lowering the lid before the creature could escape. "I have to do it. I'll be back. Be good and wait here."

Then she turned around and walked out of her room and towards the kitchen. She knew the coffer was thick enough to drown out the sounds of the hatchling, and yet she felt like it followed her. Not the sounds of it, but the feeling of it. The presence. Like a thread pulling at her, urging her to get back. She ignored it and focused on her current mission: find meat.

[[OOC: Poor Prince, but what else could Aurelie do? She couldn't have him roam her bedroom freely or go out with her. And she still is focused on the present and hasn't even started thinking of the larger implications. That the dragon needs to be taken to Fae realms.]]

And the fact that she apologized to it? Already treating it like a being with feelings, not an animal or a problem. That's the bond writing itself before she even understands what's happening.

And yes — the larger implications are going to hit her like a wall tomorrow when she's sleep-deprived and terrified and has a growing dragon in a velvet box. But tonight she's just a girl sneaking to the kitchen for meat. I love that. Let's go. 🔥]]

The Delacroix household breathed in its sleep.

Floorboards ticked and settled in the summer heat, the old timber expanding and contracting with the rhythm of a house that had stood for four generations of port lords. Moonlight fell through the tall windows of the upper corridor in pale rectangles, illuminating dust motes and the faded edges of tapestries that depicted ships, trade routes, prosperous harbors — the Delacroix legacy stitched in thread and ambition. Every door along the family wing was closed. Behind one, the youngest boy murmured something in his sleep and turned over, bed ropes creaking. Behind another, Lord Delacroix's snoring rumbled low and steady as a tide coming in.

The stairs were the worst of it. The third step from the top groaned like a wounded animal under any weight at all — the entire household knew it, stepped over it by reflex during daylight hours. In the dark, with only moonlight to navigate by, it was a trap waiting to announce every footfall to anyone still awake.

The kitchen occupied the ground floor's eastern wing, accessible through a narrow service corridor that smelled of dried rosemary and yesterday's bread. At this hour it was a cavern of copper and shadow — pots hanging from ceiling hooks like sleeping bats, the great iron stove still radiating the ghost of the evening's heat. Embers glowed dull orange in the hearth, casting just enough light to distinguish shapes: the long prep table scarred with knife marks, the row of ceramic crocks along the far wall, the pantry door standing half-open on its leather hinges.

The butcher's block sat near the pantry entrance, scrubbed clean but carrying the permanent iron-dark stain of years of use. On the shelf beside it, covered with a damp cloth and a weighted board to keep the cats out, sat tomorrow's breakfast provisions — already portioned by Cook before she'd retired. A joint of cold mutton. A crock of salted pork. A dish of chicken livers set aside for the morning's pâté, their surfaces gleaming dark and wet in the ember-light.

Something moved in the far corner.

A shape shifted near the hearth — a blanket, a straw pallet, and beneath them the broad, flour-dusted frame of Mathilde, the kitchen girl, who slept beside the stove every night from May through September because the dormitory above the stables was unbearable in summer heat. She was sixteen, built like a bread loaf, and slept the way she worked — heavily, completely, with the kind of commitment that suggested a cannon might not wake her. But might not was not would not, and she lay barely ten feet from the butcher's block, one thick arm thrown over her eyes, breathing in slow, whistling pulls through her open mouth.

The embers popped. A log shifted in the grate, sending a tiny shower of sparks across the hearthstones. Mathilde grumbled, scratched her nose without opening her eyes, and rolled toward the wall.

The chicken livers sat uncovered beneath their weighted board. The mutton joint rested on its platter. The pantry door hung open, its hinges silent, revealing darker shapes within — hanging sausages, a salt box, a rack of smoked fish wrapped in cheesecloth.

The kitchen waited, warm and close and smelling of rosemary and old blood, while the ember-light painted everything the color of rust.

Aurelie moved with slow, deliberate confidence. Countless dancing lessons had taught her that hesitation was where mistakes lived. The training had left her nimble on her feet, and she knew every nook and cranny of the house.

She dodged the third step, slipped into the kitchen, and navigated her way around Mathilde. She paused at the pantry door. Whatever meat she took wouldn't go unnoticed. The Cook would probably blame Mathilde—either for taking the meat herself or for letting an animal get into the pantry and steal it. Aurelie felt a pang of pity for the girl, but she had no other choice. Whatever punishment the Cook devised would be nothing compared to the disaster of a starving dragon escaping and revealing itself.

Aurelie opted for the chicken livers. She didn't take them all—just a few—wrapping them in a scrap of cloth she’d snagged on the way. The dragon was small; it likely wouldn't eat that much. She would have to procure more meat tomorrow. And the day after that.

Aurelie shoved those thoughts aside as Mathilde stirred again. Aurelie nearly stepped on the girl’s palm, which now rested on the floor.

Focus, Aura, she told herself. Solve the problem for now; leave the rest to tomorrow-you.

Back in her bedroom, when she lifted the lid of the coffer, the dragon launched itself out, wings rustling as it scrambled up her chest, its little talons digging into the robe.

"It's alright. Everything is fine. I'm here now." She crooned to it, one hand holding the dragon against her chest, the other gripping the cloth-wrapped meat. She carried the writhing, chirping, growling creature toward the bed and watched it devour the six chicken livers in seconds. It looked at her, puzzled, turning its head with a bird-like twitch. Aurelie smiled and shrugged.

"That's all I was able to get today. I'm sorry. If you can tolerate cured meats or eggs, I can snatch you something from breakfast. Otherwise… I'll figure something out. I won't let you starve."

She began stroking the top of the dragon's wing again, and the creature seemed to lean into it. She folded the cloth, tucked it beneath the bed, and slid under her sheets. The dragon settled on the pillow again.

"You're so pretty," she murmured sleepily, watching its scales opalesce in the moonlight.

The dragon chirped. It seemed to agree.

Then, finally, sleep took Aurelie.

Orchestrated morning scene revealing household pressure while Aurelie conceals dragon.

Dawn came too early and without mercy.

The harbor bell struck five — a low, bronze note that rolled through the port city's narrow streets and rattled the leaded glass in every window of the Delacroix estate. It was followed, as it was every morning, by the shriek of gulls fighting over fishing scraps at the eastern docks and the heavy tread of Cook's boots on the kitchen flagstones as she began her day the way she'd begun every day for twenty-three years: by cursing the state of her hearth and putting water on to boil.

Mathilde was already up, kneeling by the grate, blowing embers back to life with the steady, puffing determination of a bellows made flesh. Cook — a woman named Gerda whose arms were thicker than most men's thighs and whose opinions about food waste bordered on religious conviction — surveyed her domain with the sharp, proprietary gaze of a general inspecting a battlefield.

It took her exactly four minutes to find the discrepancy.

**"Mathilde."**

The kitchen girl flinched so hard she nearly put her face in the embers. "Ma'am?"

"The livers." Gerda stood before the butcher's block, the weighted board in one hand, the damp cloth in the other, staring at the dish with an expression that suggested someone had personally insulted her mother. "I portioned eight. There are two."

"I didn't — I was sleeping, I swear on my —"

"Six livers don't sprout legs and walk to the harbor, girl." Gerda set the board down with a crack that made the copper pots swing on their hooks. "Was the door latched?"

"I — I think —"

"You think." The word carried the weight of a sentence already passed. "If I find you've been feeding that stray tabby again, I will nail the pantry shut and you can explain to Lord Delacroix why his breakfast is bread and regret."

Mathilde's eyes welled. She opened her mouth, closed it, and returned to the hearth with the hunched posture of someone who understood that innocence and proof of innocence were entirely different currencies in this household. Gerda muttered something about girls and standards and began pulling eggs from the cold shelf with the aggressive efficiency of a woman rearranging her morning around someone else's crime.

The pâté would be an omelette instead. Gerda would make it exceptional, because Gerda's pride permitted nothing less, but the alteration would sit in her chest like a coal all day.

Upstairs, the household stirred in its usual sequence. Lord Delacroix's valet knocked at precisely half past five. The boys' tutor arrived through the servants' entrance at quarter to six, boots still damp with morning dew, clutching a leather satchel and the faintly desperate expression of a man tasked with teaching Latin to three children who would rather be throwing rocks at the harbor seals. Lady Delacroix emerged from her chamber already dressed, already assembled — hair pinned, posture immaculate, the thin smile of a woman who had been rehearsing today's performance since before she opened her eyes.

Today was the farewell breakfast for Queen Ismena's remaining envoy — the last of the formal delegation that had delivered the betrothal gifts. By noon they would depart, carrying with them a letter from Lord Delacroix confirming the wedding date and a miniature portrait of Aurelie that Lady Delacroix had commissioned three months ago from the city's best painter. The painter had softened the set of Aurelie's jaw and widened her eyes and produced something that looked like Aurelie's more agreeable cousin. Lady Delacroix had been delighted.

"Lilly," Lady Delacroix's voice carried down the corridor, clipped and bright, as she paused outside her daughter's door. "Has Aurelie risen? The envoy breakfasts at seven. She needs to be dressed and downstairs by half past six at the latest. The blue silk, I think — the one with the pearl buttons. And her hair up. She looked lovely with it up at the Hargrove dinner."

Lilly appeared from the servants' stair, already carrying a pitcher of warm water and a pressed cloth. "Not yet, my lady. Shall I wake her?"

"Please. And remind her about the tonic — she forgot it last night." Lady Delacroix smoothed an invisible wrinkle from her sleeve. "She needs color in her cheeks. The envoy will report back to the Queen, and I won't have Ismena thinking we've sent her a ghost."

Lilly curtsied and approached the door. She reached for the handle, turned it, and found it latched from inside.

A small pause. Lilly's brow creased — not with suspicion, not yet, but with the faint confusion of encountering something out of routine. Aurelie never latched her door. Not once in the years Lilly had served her.

She knocked softly. "My lady? It's Lilly. Your mother wants you dressed for breakfast. I've brought your wash water."

The corridor stretched behind her, sunlit and expectant. Lady Delacroix's heels clicked toward the staircase. Somewhere below, Gerda's voice rose in fresh accusation over the omelette pan.

Lilly knocked again, a touch louder.

"My lady?"

Aurelie stirred, the mark on her palm still stinging with echoes of pain and something else. Being a light sleeper, her eyes opened the instant she heard the door handle press down. The first thing she saw was a pair of azure blue eyes fixed on her. Then came a yawn, revealing a set of teeth that were pointy and sharp as razors as the dragon stretched.

Dragon.

Aurelie sat up straight, fully awake and painfully aware of Lilly on the other side of the door.

"Blast," she muttered, knowing her mother would have her kneeling on dried peas if she’d heard that.

"I'm awake, Lilly!" she called back, scrambling to her feet and scooping the dragon from her bed. She carried it to the coffer; the animal tried to shriek the moment it realized where it was going, but Aurelie clamped her free hand over its muzzle.

"I have to hide you. If she sees you, she'll panic. Stay there and be quiet, and I promise I'll bring you more meat later."

She didn't give herself time to feel pity for the creature as she latched the lid on its temporary prison. She walked over to the door and let Lilly in.

"Thank you for waiting, Lilly. I thought it proper to start setting some boundaries, since I'll be sleeping in my husband's chambers soon." She forced her face into cold neutrality, even as her heart squeezed. Lilly was the closest thing Aurelie had ever had to a friend, and pushing her away like this hurt. But she couldn't have Lilly barging into her bedroom anymore.

Aurelie had no idea what she would do once the dragon grew too large to be hidden in a coffer. Or if it would grow. Or how much. Or when. She knew nothing of dragon biology, other than the images in the books she’d read of enormous beasts torching villages and stealing maidens.

His knife moved through cartilage with a wet, precise crack.
